title: UK MPs call for an AI safety law and a regulator able to pause risky AI models
excerpt: A House of Commons committee lists ten gaps in UK AI oversight and asks for an AI Safety and Security Bill. The recommendations are not binding.

sources.title: Resultsense: Commons committee calls for AI safety bill and new regulator
FourWeekMBA: UK MPs list 10 AI safety gaps, want power to halt models

body_html:
A committee of the UK House of Commons has asked the government to bring in an AI Safety and Security Bill and to create a regulator with powers to pause or stop high-risk AI systems. Its report, "Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe", was published on 18 November 2026 by the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee.

Select committees are cross-party groups of MPs that examine government policy. Their reports are recommendations, not law. According to reports on the publication, the government has not committed to the proposed bill. The committee's own report page could not be opened for this story, so the details below come from two published summaries of the report and its announcement.

What the committee proposes

The committee wants the bill introduced in the next session of Parliament. It proposes a new regulator, separate from the UK's AI Security Institute, which would continue to provide technical evidence. According to the summaries, the regulator would have legal powers to:

  • require independent checks of developers' safety claims;
  • pause high-risk training and testing;
  • delay or prohibit the release of a system;
  • suspend services where risks cannot be controlled.

Resultsense reports that a material change to a system's capabilities or safeguards would trigger a fresh assessment. The committee also asks developers of designated high-risk systems to give independent evaluators meaningful access, and says it is gathering evidence on a possible international convention on AI safety and security.

The ten gaps

The committee lists ten gaps in current oversight:

  1. no definitions of unacceptable harms or risk thresholds;
  2. no legal power to access models;
  3. no independent checking of developers' safety claims;
  4. weak controls on training, testing, internal use and containment;
  5. no required, independently reviewed safety assessment before high-risk systems are released;
  6. no required reporting of incidents and near misses;
  7. no power to restrict or halt unsafe development and release;
  8. too few safeguards for models whose release cannot be reversed;
  9. weak liability rules and routes to redress;
  10. too little protection for whistleblowers.

The report also argues that safety supports growth, citing estimates that AI could make the UK economy up to £400 billion larger after ten years. Committee chair Liam Byrne MP said, as quoted by Resultsense, that the UK "cannot give today's AI leaders unfettered freedom". Senior representatives of several leading AI developers gave evidence to the inquiry, which opened in October 2026.

What is still unknown

The summaries do not give a cost or a name for the proposed regulator, or define which systems would count as high-risk. The government normally replies to select committee reports, but no response has been published yet. The UK already plans separate rules for AI agents in critical services through its Cyber Security and Resilience Bill.

Why it matters for people staying in charge

Several of the committee's gaps match the Humasure Directives: a power to pause or halt a system reflects always stoppable (D1); independent checks, incident reporting, liability and whistleblower protection reflect accountable (D9); and fresh assessments when a system changes reflect safe for its whole life (D10). Whether these become law in the UK now depends on the government's response and on Parliament.
